transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in—what brings you here today?

I’m here because my sleep has gotten really unreliable. Even when I’m exhausted and go to bed, I just lie there replaying work forecasts and issues with my team. Then I wake up around three or four in the morning and can’t get my brain to shut down again.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed you're feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed feeling sad or hopeless most of the day.
Besides work issues, do you find yourself worrying excessively about several different things—like health, family, or finances—and having a hard time controlling or stopping that worry?

Yes. I try to tell myself, “Brenda, you’ve made the plan, just let it go,” but five minutes later I’m right back in another loop. I’ll get one concern settled in my head, and then three more pop up. It’s really hard to stop once it starts.
How long have you been experiencing this pattern of excessive, hard-to-control worry—has it been going on for six months or more?
Yes. It’s been building since the sales division reorganization, about thirteen months ago.
Do you often feel restless, keyed up, or on edge during the day, separate from your sleep difficulties?
Yes. I feel wound up almost all the time—like I’m in a pipeline review even when I’m just at home eating dinner. My shoulders stay tight no matter how much I try to relax.
On nights when your mind isn't caught up in worries, do you still have trouble falling or staying asleep?
Even when I’m exhausted, I’ll lie there replaying forecasts or things going on with my team. Then I wake up around three or four, and it feels like my brain just won’t power down again.

latest_inference.note: Patient denies persistent sadness/hopelessness, ruling out major depressive disorder features. Confirmed excessive, hard-to-control worry >6 months (13 months), muscle tension, restlessness, and sleep disturbance directly tied to worry—all core GAD criteria. Sleep difficulty appears secondary to worry cognition rather than an independent primary insomnia disorder, so G47.00 is no longer supported as a separate diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient endorses chronic (13-month), excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple domains (work, general life concerns), accompanied by associated symptoms of muscle tension, feeling restless/keyed-up, and sleep disturbance (initial and middle insomnia).
